answers: A New Jersey court on Wednesday gave the Flight Crew—aka the New York Jets cheerleaders—something to cheer about: a $325,000 settlement of the class-action lawsuit filed in 2014 by a cheerleader identified as Krystal C., CNNMoney reports. That amounts to each of the 52 cheerleaders getting $2,500 per season worked and $400 per photo shoot. The settlement covers the 2012-13 and 2013-14 seasons. New York State Sen. Diane Savino, per the New York Post, cheered the settlement, calling on the NFL to "develop uniform rules … to ensure that all cheerleaders in every state received the employee pay and protections they deserve." NFL teams have sought to justify low pay for cheerleaders by saying they're independent contractors, CNN notes. In the case of the Flight Crew, Krystal C.'s suit claimed that cheerleaders were compensated $150 per game and $100 for special appearances. But, when you factor in practices and rehearsals, that pans out to $3.77 per hour. Throw in hair, makeup, and transportation expenses and "the hourly rate goes below $1.50 an hour," says the cheerleaders' attorney. The Flight Crew isn't alone: Cheerleaders have taken to the courts to seek higher pay from the Cincinnati Bengals (tentative agreement reached), Tampa Bay Buccaneers (settled for $825,000), Oakland Raiders (settled for $1.25 million), and the Buffalo Bills (class-action suit on the horizon).

full.prediction:
**Summary of News:**

The New York Jets cheerleaders, known as the Flight Crew, have reached a settlement with the team in a class-action lawsuit over fair pay and working conditions. The $325,000 settlement, approved by a New Jersey court, was initially agreed upon in August 2015 and finalized in 2016. The deal covers the 2012-13 and 2013-14 NFL seasons and provides each of the 52 cheerleaders with $2,500 per season they worked. Cheerleaders who participated in photo shoots are also eligible for an additional $400 per shoot. The settlement includes interest and will be adjusted based on the number of seasons each cheerleader worked.

The lawsuit, led by former cheerleader Krystal C., alleged that the cheerleaders were paid only $150 per game and $100 for special events, with no compensation for weekly practices or rehearsals. The Jets denied the claims, stating that the settlement was reached to avoid the costs and disruption of litigation. The cheerleaders' attorney, Patricia Pierce, argued that the actual hourly wage was far below the minimum wage, with some cheerleaders earning as little as $1.50 per hour when factoring in expenses like hair, makeup, and transportation.

This case is part of a broader trend of NFL cheerleaders fighting for fair pay and employee rights. Similar lawsuits have been filed against other teams, including the Cincinnati Bengals, Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Oakland Raiders, and Buffalo Bills. The Buccaneers settled for $825,000, the Bengals have reached a tentative agreement, and the Raiders settled for $1.25 million in 2014. The Buffalo Bills' cheerleaders, known as the Jills, have also been granted class-action status in a similar wage suit.

State Senator Diane Savino (D-SI) praised the Jets' settlement and called for other NFL teams, including the Bills, to follow suit. She urged the NFL to establish uniform rules to ensure all cheerleaders across the league receive fair pay and employee protections. The ongoing legal battles highlight the growing recognition of cheerleaders as employees rather than independent contractors, with courts increasingly rejecting the teams' attempts to classify them as such.
